Designer Friend

A structured learning platform for self-taught designers, where the product writes none of the lessons. Its whole value is the order it puts free tutorials in, and the proof that you're moving through them.

{{ m.k }}
{{ m.v }}
The problem

Not a lack of resources. A lack of guidance.

Becoming a designer is more accessible than ever, and that accessibility created the problem. Beginners aren't starving for information; they're drowning in it. A search for "UX basics" returns a firehose. Learners jump between disconnected resources without ever making tangible progress, mistake popularity for quality, and tackle topics in whatever order the algorithm serves them. Because the learning is scattered, there's no place where any of it accumulates, so effort produces no visible result.

Designers don't need more information; they need the right information, in the right order. That points at what the product has to be good at: choosing, ordering, and making effort visible. Not producing.

  1. 01 No sequence. Without a curriculum, learners tackle topics out of order and end up with isolated skills that never connect into a process a job asks for.
  2. 02 No quality signal. Popularity is the only signal a beginner can read, and popularity measures reach, not accuracy, not currency.
  3. 03 No accumulation. Learning spread across disconnected resources leaves no trace. Nothing adds up, so progress feels invisible and motivation goes with it.
Method

How I framed this without users

No users were interviewed and nothing here has been usability-tested.
  1. 01 Secondary research across online design communities, looking at how self-taught designers describe where they get stuck rather than what they say they want.
  2. 02 Analysis of the problem space, breaking a general complaint into three separate failures (sequence, quality signal, accumulation) so each could get its own answer in the product.
  3. 03 Two proto-personas built from that material, used as a framing device for design decisions rather than presented as findings.

Everything below is a design judgment, not a measurement. That distinction is kept visible throughout.

Who I designed for

Two proto-personas, both derived from secondary research rather than interviews. Designing for both meant one product with two different entry speeds.

Maya's needs shaped the core: roadmaps as the primary object, a stated sequence, progress made visible. Leo is served at the edges: Latest Trends, the blog, bookmarks.

The approach

3 key design moves

  1. 01 Made the path finite. Every roadmap states its length, its weekly cost and its endpoint before anyone starts.
  2. 02 Put progress above the curriculum. Hours spent and lessons completed sit at the top of the course screen, with a Next Step module naming the single upcoming action.
  3. 03 Contained the curriculum. Lessons are grouped into expandable units, so the shape of the path stays visible without all of it being exposed at once.
Information architecture
Key design decisions

Five decisions that shaped Designer Friend

These five address the three failures above. Blogs, Latest Trends and the certificate extend the product; none of them matters if a structured path with visible progress isn't enough to keep someone learning.

01

The product asks for nothing until you've seen the path

The problem

A visitor whose defining problem is not knowing where to start can't evaluate a product that won't let them look.

The design

The structure splits at one line: everything public exists to explain, everything behind it exists to sequence and track. The headline states the promise and stays discipline-neutral, "Your friendly guide to learning design in the right order." The CTA reads "Explore Designer Friend" with downward arrows: an invitation to scroll, not a demand to commit.

Why it works this way

The product's value is legibility. Asking for commitment before someone has seen a single path inverts what's being sold. The landing page is doing qualification work, not conversion work; its job is to let the wrong visitor leave and the right one keep scrolling.

  1. 1→Names no discipline, the promise, not the field
  2. 2→Explore, not Sign up
  3. Costs: A discipline-neutral headline says nothing above the fold about which fields the platform covers, so a graphic or motion designer has to scroll to find out. And the roadmap catalogue itself sits behind sign-up, the boundary I'd move first.
  4. Validate: Whether a visitor scrolls at all on a headline that names nothing specific to them.
02

A path states its cost before you start it

The problem

"Learn UX" isn't a decision anyone can make. Open-ended learning gives no way to judge what you're committing to, which is how people end up abandoning something they never sized in the first place.

The design

Roadmap cards carry discipline, duration and weekly time commitment alongside the Start now action, 6 weeks, 4 hrs per week. The roadmap detail opens with "What you'll learn," and every path ends in a final project.

Why it works this way

A path with an end is a different proposition from a library. Stating the cost up front lets someone match a roadmap against the time they actually have, and it's what makes the progress modules meaningful later; you can only measure progress against something with a defined size.

  1. 1→Duration
  2. 2→Weekly commitment
  3. 3→Start now
  4. Costs: A stated duration is a promise the platform can't keep for everyone. Someone slower than the estimate is now behind on a schedule they didn't set, which risks producing exactly the discouragement the product exists to prevent.
  5. Validate: Whether duration is what people actually choose between roadmaps on, or whether they ignore it for the topic, and whether falling behind it demotivates.
03

The core screen is ordered: where you are → what's next → what's left

The problem

Two of the three failures land on this one screen. Progress is invisible, and a curriculum is structurally a long list, so the screen built to fix overwhelm is also the screen most likely to cause it.

The design

Course Progress sits above the lesson list, counting three things separately: hours spent, lessons completed, projects made. Next Step names the specific upcoming lesson with a single Resume button and the endpoint attached, finish the roadmap and the final project to unlock the certificate. Below that, lessons are grouped into expandable units under All Lessons, with Bookmarks as a second view.

Why it works this way

The ordering is the decision. A returning learner sees what they've accomplished before they see what remains. Hours matter as much as percentage: someone fitting learning around a job controls time given, not lessons completed, and a completion bar credits none of it. Naming the next lesson rather than showing a generic "continue" means resuming costs one click and no scanning.

  1. 1→Three metrics
  2. 2→Next Step naming the lesson
  3. 3→Collapsed units
  4. 4→Certificate endpoint
  5. 5→All Lessons / Bookmarks tabs
  6. Costs: Three metrics plus a Next Step module push the curriculum below the fold on smaller screens. Expandable units also make the full syllabus harder to scan, which is why "What you'll learn" has to carry that load one level up.
  7. Validate: Whether someone can describe their own progress without opening the lesson list. And whether people open every unit immediately, if they do, they want the overview and the wrong thing is collapsed.
04

Progress has to survive leaving the roadmap

The problem

The motivation loop breaks between roadmaps, not inside them. Someone who pauses one path and starts another has no place where any of it adds up, the original failure reproduced one level higher.

The design

The profile carries a Your Learning Progress section listing every roadmap started with its completion percentage and a Resume action, a monthly hours-spent bar graph, and completed certificates.

Why it works this way

Inside a roadmap, progress is a percentage. Across roadmaps it's a record. The bar graph turns time given into something visible over months rather than sessions, and the list of started-but-unfinished paths is a standing reminder rather than something the learner has to hold in their head.

  1. 1→Every roadmap started, with % and Resume
  2. 2→Hours by month
  3. 3→Certificates
  4. Costs: A list of unfinished roadmaps is honest, but it's also a list of things you haven't done, the same surface reads as a record or an accusation depending on how many entries sit at 20%. An hours graph also rewards time rather than outcome, which is gameable by leaving a video running.
  5. Validate: Whether the profile gets used as a re-entry point or only as a summary, and whether seeing several stalled roadmaps encourages return or discourages it.
05

The product runs at two speeds

The problem

A learning product made only of roadmaps loses people between them. And it has nothing for someone who already knows the fundamentals and needs to fill specific gaps.

The design

Roadmaps are the slow speed: sequential, committed, finite. The blog is a reading surface with its own screen, and because the posts come from elsewhere, each card carries a discipline tag the original headline doesn't. Latest Trends is smaller on purpose: six picks on the landing page, no archive and no index, each one opening straight into a tutorial.

Why it works this way

"What should I learn next" is a roadmap question. "What's happening in the industry right now" isn't, and forcing it into a sequence would make it stale by construction. The tags supply the signal the source material doesn't carry, the same move the roadmaps make with tutorials, at a smaller scale.

  1. 1→Discipline tags
  2. 2→A trend card, no duration, no sequence, nothing to commit to
  3. Costs: This is the only part of the product serving the second user type, and it's a content shelf rather than a path. It gives Leo somewhere to land but no way in at his level, the clearest unfinished part of the concept.
  4. Validate: Whether anyone moves between the two speeds, or whether the fast lane simply competes with the roadmap for the same attention.
System thinking

Design system

Typography
Inter

A learning product is mostly lesson titles, descriptions and progress figures set at small sizes and read in sequence. Inter carries that density without the interface competing with the content it's organising.

Color
{{ c.hex }}
{{ c.name }}

The accents are surface colours, not content colours: each carries ink at between 9.7:1 and 12:1, so text and icons sit inside accent blocks rather than being coloured by them. A coloured area is never defined by colour alone; it carries dark content or a border.

Components

The lesson row is the highest-value component: it appears in All Lessons, in Bookmarks, and as the learning-progress card in the profile: three contexts, three states, one structure. Building it before the screens meant later screens became compositions rather than drawings.

The section message carries four states (info, error, warning, success) so feedback is a defined part of the library rather than improvised per screen.

Honest limitations

What I'd validate next

Designer Friend is a concept. These decisions are hypotheses, not conclusions. If it moved toward a real product, the first priority would be moderated sessions with 5–7 participants across both user types.

Beyond exploratory sessions, a real product would need completion and return-rate data before any of these decisions could be treated as settled.
